en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Saṅghādisesa Offenses.
10. The Training Rule on Schism in the Saṅgha.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then Devadatta went to Kokālika, Kaṭamodakatissaka, Samuddadatta the son of Khaṇḍadevī, and...
He approached them; having approached, he said this to Kokālika, Kaṭamorakatissaka, and Samuddadatta, the son of Khaṇḍadevī:
"Come, friends, let us cause a schism in the Saṅgha of the ascetic Gotama, a breaking of the wheel.
When this was said, Kokālika said this to Devadatta:
“Friends, the ascetic Gotama is of great psychic power and great majesty.
How can we cause a schism in the Saṅgha of the ascetic Gotama, a schism in the Wheel?
“Come, friends, let us approach the ascetic Gotama and request five points.”
“Bhante, the Blessed One has in many ways praised fewness of desires, contentment, effacement, the ascetic practices, serenity, reduction of burdens, and the arousal of energy.
Bhante, these five things lead in many ways to fewness of desires, contentment, effacement, the ascetic practices, serenity, reduction of burdens, and the arousal of energy.
It would be well, Bhante, if the bhikkhus...”
For as long as life lasts, they should be forest-dwellers;
whoever should enter a village settlement, let a fault touch him.
For as long as life lasts, they should be alms-food eaters.
Whoever should accept an invitation, fault would touch him.
For as long as life lasts they should be rag-robe wearers;
whoever should accept a robe from a householder, fault would touch him.
For as long as life lasts, they should be tree-root dwellers;
whoever should resort to a roofed dwelling would incur an offense.
For as long as life lasts, they should not eat fish or meat.
‘Whoever should eat fish and meat would incur blame.
The ascetic Gotama will not permit these things.
With these five points we shall convince the people.”
"Friends, it is indeed possible to cause a schism in the Saṅgha and a breaking of the Wheel of the ascetic Gotama by means of these five grounds.
For people, friends, are inclined toward what is coarse.
Then Devadatta, together with his retinue, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, Devadatta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, in many ways the Blessed One speaks in praise of one who has few desires … [and so on] … of one who exerts energy.”
"Venerable sir, these five things lead in many ways to fewness of desires...
[and so on] ...to the arousal of energy.
It would be good, venerable sir, if the bhikkhus were forest-dwellers for as long as life lasts."
“Whoever should enter a village would be touched by blame...
[and so on] ...if they were to abstain from fish and meat for as long as life lasts, whoever should eat fish and meat would be touched by blame.
“Enough, Devadatta!”
Whoever wishes, let him be a forest-dweller; whoever wishes, let him dwell near a village.
Whoever wishes, let him be an alms-food eater; whoever wishes, let him accept invitations.
Whoever wishes, let him be a wearer of rag-robes; whoever wishes, let him accept robes from householders.
“Devadatta, for eight months I have authorized the lodging at the foot of a tree and fish and meat that are pure in three respects:
not seen, not heard, and not suspected.
Then Devadatta—

“The Blessed One does not authorize these five points. Delighted and elated, Devadatta rose from his seat together with his followers, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed.
Then Devadatta, having entered Rājagaha with his followers, persuaded the people by means of the five points:
“Friends, we approached the ascetic Gotama and requested these five points.”
“Bhante, the Blessed One has in many ways praised fewness of desires, contentment, effacement, asceticism, serenity, reduction of burdens, and the arousal of energy.
Bhante, these five things lead in many ways to fewness of desires, contentment, effacement, asceticism, serenity, reduction of burdens, and the arousal of energy.
It would be good, Bhante, if the bhikkhus were forest-dwellers for as long as life lasts.”
Whoever should enter a village would incur a fault.
Let them be alms-food eaters for as long as life lasts;
whoever should accept an invitation would incur a fault.
"For as long as life lasts, they should be wearers of rag-robes;
whoever should accept a robe from a householder, let a fault touch him.
For as long as life lasts, they should be dwellers at the foot of a tree;"
‘Whoever should resort to what is concealed would incur blame;
for as long as life lasts they should not eat fish or meat;
whoever should eat fish or meat would incur blame.’”
“The ascetic Gotama does not permit these things;
yet we have undertaken and are practicing ourselves according to these five points.
Thereupon, those people who were faithless, lacking confidence, and of poor understanding spoke thus:
“Indeed, these ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, are austere and live lives of effacement;
but the ascetic Gotama is luxurious and intends for luxury.
However, those people who were faithful, confident, wise, competent, and intelligent, complained, criticized, and spoke out against this.
"How indeed can Devadatta strive for the schism of the Blessed One’s Saṅgha, for the breaking of the Wheel?
The monks heard those people who were thus complaining, grumbling, and lamenting.
Those monks who were of few desires... [they] complained, grumbled, and lamented:
“How indeed can Devadatta strive for a schism in the Saṅgha, for a breaking of the wheel?
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked Devadatta in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ...“Is it true, Devadatta, that you are striving for a schism in the Saṅgha, for a breaking of the wheel?”
“It is true, Blessed One,” he replied.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, strive for a schism in the Saṅgha, for a schism in the Wheel?”
“Monk, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence… And thus,
monks, you should recite this training rule:

‘Whatever monk should strive for the schism of a harmonious Saṅgha, or should persist in taking up and maintaining a legal issue conducive to schism, that monk should be addressed by the monks thus:’”
‘Venerable sir, do not strive for a schism in a united Saṅgha, nor persist in taking up and maintaining a legal issue conducive to a schism. Let the venerable one be reconciled with the Saṅgha;
for a united Saṅgha, living in harmony, without dispute, and following a single recitation, dwells in comfort.

If that bhikkhu, being thus addressed by the bhikkhus, should still persist as before, that bhikkhu is to be formally admonished by the bhikkhus up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that position.
"If, after being admonished up to three times, he should relinquish it, that is good;
if he should not relinquish it, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
As for "whoever":
Whoever is such...
[as described] ...a bhikkhu... this is the bhikkhu intended in this context.
"United" means the Saṅgha is of common residence and stands within the same boundary.
"Should strive for a schism" means—
Thinking, "How might these [monks] become divided, separated, and factionalized? he seeks out a party and forms a group.
Or, regarding a legal issue that leads to schism:
this refers to the eighteen bases for causing a schism.
"Having undertaken" means having taken up.
"Having exerted" means...
He would kindle it.
"He would persist" means he would not relinquish it.
"Thus, 'a bhikkhu' refers to that bhikkhu who causes a schism in the Saṅgha.
'By the bhikkhus' refers to— "
Other monks who see or hear of it should say to him:
"Venerable sir, do not strive for the schism of a united Saṅgha, nor stand up having taken up and maintained a legal issue conducive to schism.
Let the Venerable one be reconciled with the Saṅgha."
"For the Saṅgha, being united, harmonious, and without dispute, with a single recitation, dwells in comfort.
This should be said a second time;
it should be said a third time.
If he relinquishes it, that is good;
if he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Having heard [the charge], if they do not speak, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Then that bhikkhu, having been dragged even into the midst of the Saṅgha, should be told:
“Venerable sir, do not strive for the schism of a harmonious Saṅgha, nor stand up having taken up and maintained a legal issue conducive to schism.
Let the venerable one be reconciled with the Saṅgha.”
"For the Saṅgha, being united, living in harmony, and free from dispute, with a single recitation of the rules, dwells in comfort.
This should be said a second time;
it should be said a third time.
If he relinquishes it, that is good;
if he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
That bhikkhu is to be formally admonished:
“And furthermore, monks, he should be admonished in this way:
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.’”
This monk named so-and-so is striving for a schism in the harmonious Saṅgha.
He does not relinquish that course of action.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha formally admonish the monk named so-and-so so that he may relinquish that course of action.
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs:
this monk named so-and-so is striving for the schism of the harmonious Saṅgha.
Thus he does not relinquish that matter.
The Saṅgha formally admonishes the monk named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
Whichever venerable one approves of the formal admonition of the monk named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter, let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve of this, let him speak.
For the second time I speak this matter...
for the third time I speak this matter: [whoever does not approve of this, let him speak].
Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This monk named so-and-so is striving for a schism in the harmonious Saṅgha;
he does not relinquish that course of action.
The Saṅgha formally admonishes the bhikkhu named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
Whichever venerable one approves of the formal admonition of the bhikkhu named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“Bhikkhu so-and-so has been dealt with by the Saṅgha for the relinquishing of that matter.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent.
Thus do I understand this.”
For the motion, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
for two proclamations, there are offenses of serious transgression;
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension from the Saṅgha.
For one who commits a *saṅghādisesa* offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the motion; with two proclamations, the serious offenses (*thullaccaya*) are extinguished.
"A *saṅghādisesa*" ...
[as before] ... for that reason also it is called a *saṅghādisesa*.

If, regarding a legitimate legal procedure (*dhammakamma*), one perceives it as a legitimate legal procedure and does not relinquish [the offense], there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
If, regarding a legitimate legal procedure, one is uncertain and does not relinquish it, there is an offense entailing suspension.
If, regarding a legitimate legal procedure, one perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure (*adhammakamma*) and does not relinquish it, there is an offense entailing suspension.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as a legitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one is doubtful about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense for one who does not admonish,
or for one who relinquishes [the matter].
For one who is insane,
for one whose mind is deranged,
for one overwhelmed by pain.
"For one who is a first offender":
thus ends the tenth training rule concerning schism in the Sangha.
